title: Medical conditions that affect dental care
blurb: Diabetes, bleeding risks, bisphosphonates, epilepsy, heart conditions, pregnancy and dry mouth: how each changes dental care, and why an up-to-date medical history matters.
question: You are updating the medical history of a 67-year-old booked for an extraction. She takes warfarin for an irregular heartbeat, alendronic acid once a week for osteoporosis, and metformin for type 2 diabetes. Which of these affect the extraction, and what must the dentist know before starting?

teach.h: Why the medical history comes first
teach.body: The medical history tells the dentist whether treatment is safe, how to adapt it, and which emergencies to be ready for. It must be comprehensive: conditions, all medicines (including over-the-counter and herbal), allergies, past problems with treatment, pregnancy, smoking and alcohol. It must be contemporaneous: recorded at the time, not from memory later. It is updated at each new course of treatment and checked verbally at every visit, and the dentist reviews it. You help the patient complete it, record exactly what they say and flag any change to the dentist.

teach.h: Condition → why it matters → what the team does

Dental relevance
Team action

Morning slot after a meal; glucose ready
Check INR or doses; local measures

teach.body: Diabetes and periodontitis work both ways: poorly controlled diabetes makes gum disease worse, and treating gum disease can help blood sugar control. Healing is slower, infections are more likely, and dry mouth and thrush are common. The emergency risk is hypoglycaemia (low blood sugar), especially if a meal is missed after insulin. Signs: shaky, sweaty, pale, confused or irritable. Book morning appointments soon after the patient's usual meal and medication, and check they have eaten.

teach.caption: SDCEP: check INR ideally within 24 hours (up to 72 hours if stable). Below 4, treatment can usually go ahead without stopping warfarin. Bleeding disorders such as haemophilia need liaison with the haemophilia centre.

teach.body: Antiresorptive drugs slow bone turnover. They include bisphosphonates (alendronic acid tablets for osteoporosis; zoledronic acid infusions in cancer care) and denosumab injections; some anti-angiogenic cancer drugs carry a similar risk. They can cause medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ): exposed, dead jaw bone that has not healed after 8 weeks, often after an extraction. The risk is low with osteoporosis tablets and higher with cancer doses. Bisphosphonates stay in bone for years, so always ask about past use too.

steps.label: MRONJ
steps.sub: Exposed bone not healed after 8 weeks

teach.caption: Prevention is best: get the mouth healthy before the drug starts, and avoid extractions where possible. Patients should never stop the drug unless their prescriber advises it.

teach.body: For epilepsy, record the seizure type, how often, when the last one was, and triggers such as missed medication, tiredness, stress, flashing lights or missed meals. Phenytoin can cause gingival overgrowth (so can ciclosporin and calcium-channel blockers such as nifedipine). If a convulsive seizure lasts 5 minutes or more, buccal midazolam is given. Patients with angina should bring their GTN spray. NICE does not recommend routine antibiotic cover against infective endocarditis for dental treatment; for high-risk patients the dentist may liaise with their cardiologist.

children.label: Mouth changes
children.sub: Pregnancy gingivitis, epulis, erosion from sickness

children.label: Chair care
children.sub: Late on, avoid lying flat: tilt to her left side

children.label: Entitlement
children.sub: Free NHS dental care in pregnancy and for 12 months after birth

teach.caption: Lying flat late in pregnancy lets the womb press on a major vein, so she may feel faint. Radiographs, like all exposures, must be justified.

children.label: Causes
children.sub: Medicines, head and neck radiotherapy, Sjögren's, diabetes, dehydration

children.label: Effects
children.sub: Caries (esp. root), thrush, sore mouth, loose dentures, taste change

children.label: Help
children.sub: Sip water, sugar-free gum, saliva substitutes, high-fluoride paste

teach.caption: Many common medicines dry the mouth, such as some antidepressants, antihistamines and blood pressure drugs. Taking several at once (polypharmacy) adds up.

teach.text: Never tell a patient to stop warfarin, a DOAC, aspirin or a bisphosphonate before treatment. Only the prescriber, or the dentist following SDCEP guidance, advises any change. Stopping an anticoagulant can cause a stroke.

items: Medical history: comprehensive, contemporaneous, updated each course of treatment, checked every visit.
Diabetes: perio link, slow healing; prevent and treat hypos (oral glucose 15–20 g if conscious).
Warfarin: recent INR; below 4 usually treat. Avoid suggesting ibuprofen; watch miconazole.
Bisphosphonates/denosumab: MRONJ risk after extractions; ask about past use.
Pregnancy: avoid lying flat late on. Dry mouth: high caries and thrush risk.

summary: You can now explain what makes a medical history comprehensive and contemporaneous, and describe how diabetes, bleeding disorders and anticoagulants, bisphosphonates, epilepsy, heart conditions, pregnancy and dry mouth each change dental care, including what the team must check or have ready.

A.q: A patient who takes warfarin is booked for an extraction. What does the dentist need to see before treatment?
A.why: INR measures how long the blood takes to clot in patients on warfarin. SDCEP advises checking it ideally within 24 hours of the procedure.

whyNot.0: HbA1c measures long-term blood sugar control in diabetes.
whyNot.2: Peak flow is used to monitor asthma.
whyNot.3: Cholesterol does not affect bleeding after an extraction.

A.q: Medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ) is a risk with which medicine?
A.why: Alendronic acid is a bisphosphonate. Antiresorptive drugs slow bone turnover, so sockets can fail to heal, leaving exposed dead bone.

whyNot.0: Metformin treats type 2 diabetes and does not cause MRONJ.
whyNot.1: Salbutamol is an asthma reliever inhaler.

A.q: A patient with diabetes becomes shaky, sweaty and confused in the chair but is conscious and able to swallow. What should be given first?
options: Two puffs of GTN under the tongue
A.why: A conscious patient with hypoglycaemia is given 15–20 g of oral glucose, repeated after 15 minutes if needed.

whyNot.0: Glucagon is used if the patient is unconscious or cannot swallow safely.
whyNot.1: GTN is for angina chest pain.
whyNot.3: Aspirin is for a suspected heart attack.

B.q: A patient with epilepsy has enlarged, overgrown gums. Which of her medicines is the most likely cause?
B.why: Phenytoin, an anti-epileptic drug, is a well-known cause of drug-induced gingival overgrowth.

whyNot.1: Paracetamol does not cause gum overgrowth.
whyNot.2: Amoxicillin is an antibiotic and does not cause gum overgrowth.
whyNot.3: Omeprazole reduces stomach acid and does not cause gum overgrowth.

B.q: A patient who is 34 weeks pregnant feels faint and dizzy after lying flat in the chair. What should you do?
options: Raise her legs and keep her flat
Give her oral glucose straight away
Turn her onto her left side
B.why: Late in pregnancy, lying flat lets the womb press on a major vein, reducing blood flow back to the heart. Tilting her onto her left side relieves it.

whyNot.0: Keeping her flat keeps the pressure on the vein.
whyNot.1: The quickest relief is to take the weight off the vein by tilting her to the left.
whyNot.2: This is not low blood sugar; it is pressure on a vein from lying flat.

B.q: A patient's medicines have given him a very dry mouth. Which dental problem is he at most increased risk of?
B.why: Saliva washes away sugars and buffers acid. Without it, caries risk rises sharply, especially on exposed roots and at the gum line.

whyNot.0: Fluorosis develops in childhood from too much fluoride.
whyNot.2: Amelogenesis imperfecta is inherited and present from tooth formation.
whyNot.3: Attrition comes from grinding, not dry mouth.

C.q: Why must the medical history be recorded contemporaneously?
options: So it can be written up later from memory
So it shows the patient's health at that time
So it only needs updating every five years
So the nurse can make the treatment decision
C.why: Contemporaneous means recorded at the time, so the record accurately reflects the patient's current health and medicines.

whyNot.0: Writing up later from memory is the opposite of contemporaneous and risks errors.
whyNot.2: It is updated at each course of treatment and checked at each visit.
whyNot.3: The dentist reviews the history and makes treatment decisions.

C.q: A patient with a replacement heart valve asks whether he needs antibiotics before his scale and polish. What is the current UK position?
options: Always given one hour before any treatment
Only given if the patient requests them
Given for a week after every appointment
Not routine; the dentist decides with advice
C.why: NICE does not recommend routine antibiotic prophylaxis for dental procedures. For high-risk patients the dentist may liaise with the cardiologist.

whyNot.0: Routine prophylaxis before dental treatment is no longer recommended.
whyNot.1: Antibiotics are prescribed on clinical grounds, not on request.
whyNot.2: Courses of antibiotics after treatment are not recommended and add resistance risk.

C.q: A patient with epilepsy is having a convulsive seizure that has now lasted 5 minutes. Which emergency drug is used?
C.why: Buccal midazolam (adult dose 10 mg) is given if a convulsive seizure lasts 5 minutes or more, or seizures recur in quick succession.

reteach.title: Three questions the dentist is asking
reteach.question: When the dentist reads a medical history, they are really asking: will this patient bleed, will they heal, and could they collapse? Which conditions answer each question?

blocks.body: Every condition on the form matters because it changes one of these answers. Anticoagulants and bleeding disorders change 'will they bleed?'. Bisphosphonates, diabetes, radiotherapy and smoking change 'will they heal?'. Diabetes, epilepsy, angina and asthma change 'could they collapse?', so the right emergency drug must be ready. That is why an incomplete or out-of-date history can put a patient in danger.

Diabetes (hypo), epilepsy, angina, asthma, severe allergy
Dry mouth, pregnancy, phenytoin, steroid inhalers

blocks.text: A patient saying 'nothing's changed' still needs the history checked. New medicines, especially from a hospital or bought over the counter, are easily forgotten.

explain.body: Comprehensive: conditions, all medicines including past bisphosphonates, allergies, past problems with treatment, pregnancy, smoking and alcohol. Contemporaneous: written at the time. Updated each course of treatment, checked every visit, and reviewed by the dentist.

steps.label: Patient completes form
steps.sub: Help if needed; interpreter if required

test.q: A patient lists only the medicines her GP prescribes. What else should you ask about for a comprehensive medical history?
options: Her preferred appointment days and times
test.why: All medicines matter, including over-the-counter and herbal products, because they can affect bleeding, healing or interact with drugs the dentist may use.

whyNot.1: Appointment preferences are administrative, not part of the medical history.
whyNot.2: Exemption status is recorded for NHS charges, not as medical history.
whyNot.3: Payment details are financial records, not medical history.

explain.body: Diabetes worsens gum disease and slows healing. Prevent hypos with morning appointments after a normal meal and medication. If a hypo happens, treat according to whether the patient can swallow safely.

test.q: A patient with diabetes has collapsed and is unconscious with a suspected hypo. Which drug is given?
test.why: An unconscious patient cannot swallow safely, so glucagon 1 mg is given intramuscularly and an ambulance is called.

whyNot.0: Oral glucose must not be given to an unconscious patient: choking risk.

explain.body: Warfarin needs a recent INR (ideally within 24 hours); below 4, treatment usually goes ahead. DOACs and antiplatelets are not routinely stopped; the dentist follows SDCEP guidance. Use local haemostatic measures, book early in the day, and don't suggest ibuprofen. Miconazole raises warfarin's effect.

explain.h: Before an extraction on an anticoagulant
items: Check the medicine and dose on the medical history.
Warfarin: confirm a recent INR result.
Book early in the day and week, so any bleeding can be managed.
Prepare local haemostatic aids, such as sutures and an absorbable dressing.
Give written post-op advice: pressure on a gauze pack if it bleeds.

test.q: Which painkiller should a patient on warfarin generally avoid after an extraction?
test.why: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen increase bleeding risk in patients on anticoagulants. Paracetamol is the usual choice.

whyNot.0: Paracetamol is the preferred painkiller for patients on warfarin.
whyNot.1: Codeine is not the main concern for bleeding.
whyNot.3: A topical anaesthetic gel does not increase bleeding.

explain.body: Bisphosphonates, denosumab and some cancer drugs slow bone turnover. After an extraction, the socket may not heal, leaving exposed dead bone for more than 8 weeks. Cancer doses carry a higher risk than osteoporosis tablets. Prevention and avoiding extractions are key.

items.label: exposed bone not healed: the MRONJ definition
bisphosphonates stay in bone after stopping

test.q: A patient stopped alendronic acid three years ago. Why should this still be recorded?
options: It stays in bone for years
test.why: Bisphosphonates bind to bone and stay there for years, so a past course can still affect healing after an extraction.

whyNot.0: Fluorosis is caused by excess fluoride in childhood.
whyNot.2: Gum overgrowth is linked to phenytoin, ciclosporin and calcium-channel blockers.
